catalog_quote: [Amery 2016: xiv] Stress The first syllable in Kaurna words as always stressed. In longer words, the third syllable receives secondary stress. Stress the bold syllables in Ngangkiparingga. [Amery 2016: 137] Carryover of English stress patterns is also a noticeable tendency. For instance, the Kaurna name Medika (drawn from mitika 'flower') is heard pronounced [mǝdíkʌ] rather than [mídɩkʌ] as expected. It is almost certain that Kaurna, like Nukunu, Adnyamathanha etc. regularly stressed the first syllable. Spelling pronunciations and stress placement on the second syllable are more noticeable amongst those who have had little or no contact with Kaurna language programs, and have accessed the words themselves from T&S. [Amery 2016: 166] ... to ensure that stress is placed regularly on the first syllable. [Black 1920: 80] The stressed or accented syllable is indicated by the sign ['] placed before it, but as the great majority of native words are accented on the first syllable, the accent mark is omitted whenever such is the case. ... Where there are four syllables, as in [bindjanidja], [yarinyjeri], and [jerabula], the main stress is still on the first syllable and there is a slight secondary stress on the third syllable, as in the English "tantalizing." Why certain words, such as [tan'danja, ka'rawi, pu'lombi, ba'lardu] are accented on the second syllable, is a question whose solution would require a more thorough knowledge of native languages than we possess.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every Kaurna word; in words of four or more syllables a secondary stress falls on the third syllable (alternating rhythm). The rule is stated as the norm for revived Kaurna and justified by comparison with closely related Thura-Yura languages (Nukunu, Adnyamathanha); it matches Black's (1920: 80) first-hand observation from the last speaker that 'the great majority of native words are accented on the first syllable' with 'a slight secondary stress on the third syllable' in four-syllable words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Third syllable in longer words (Amery 2016: xiv; Black 1920: 80 'slight secondary stress on the third syllable, as in the English tantalizing').
new_statements.exceptions: Amery treats second-syllable stress among learners as English carry-over/spelling pronunciation, not a Kaurna pattern. Black (1920: 80-84), transcribing Ivaritji, marks a handful of Adelaide-language items with second-syllable accent (tan'danja 'Adelaide', pata'wilja 'Glenelg', ka'vaiji 'come', taŋ'kaira, yanki'parinka) and says he cannot explain them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation forms in a language reclaimed from 19th-century written records (no sound recordings); Amery's rule is reconstructive/prescriptive for revived Kaurna (Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi 2010 spelling guide), corroborated by Black's 1919 phonetic transcription of the last L1 speaker. Amery's book is a language-reclamation monograph with a pronunciation guide rather than a full reference grammar.
new_statements.identity_note: Kaurna (kaur1267, ISO zku), the Adelaide Plains language, Thura-Yura subgroup of Pama-Nyungan. Amery 2016 describes reclaimed/revived Kaurna, whose phonology (incl. stress) is reconstructed from 19th-c. records plus closely related Nukunu and Adnyamathanha; Black 1920's 'Adelaide language' vocabulary is first-hand Kaurna from the last fluent speaker Ivaritji (Amelia Taylor), recorded at Point Pearce in 1919, but his stress remark on p.80 is phrased generally for all four vocabularies in the paper (Adelaide/Kaurna, Narungga, Kukata, Ngarrindjeri).

sources.note: Spelling/pronunciation guide p. xiv: first syllable of Kaurna words always stressed; in longer words the third syllable takes secondary stress (example Ngangkiparingga). Ch. 6 p.137: 'almost certain that Kaurna, like Nukunu, Adnyamathanha etc. regularly stressed the first syllable'; learners' second-syllable stress (e.g. Medika [mǝdíkʌ] for expected [mídɩkʌ]) treated as English carry-over; p.166 urges stress 'placed regularly on the first syllable'.
